questions.q: Why can't an enterprise with dozens of interdependent services simply fail everything over at once on live traffic and call it a DR drill?
options: Failing everything over at once on live traffic isn't a controlled drill at all — it's an outage the team scheduled for itself
Cloud providers technically prevent more than one service from failing over in the same hour
This is actually the recommended approach, and scoping tests to one service is considered outdated practice
Failing over the whole estate at once is only a problem for active-active workloads
questions.explain: Failing dozens of services over simultaneously on live production traffic isn't a controlled test — it's a self-inflicted outage, which is why real enterprise DR testing is scoped to deliberately smaller slices.

questions.q: What role does the dependency graph from Lesson 14 play in scoping a production DR test?
options: It defines the safe boundary of the test — which services and dependencies genuinely belong in that drill's blast radius, and which can be excluded and tested separately
It is only used for billing reports and has no role in test scoping
It replaces the need for any rollback plan during the test
It is used exclusively to schedule when tests occur, not to define their scope
questions.explain: The same graph that defines a real failure's blast radius defines a safe test boundary — services genuinely coupled to the one under test are included, and unrelated services are excluded and tested on their own schedule.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that testing DR against real production traffic is often necessary, rather than relying on staging alone?
options: Staging environments rarely reproduce real data volume, warmed caches, or actual third-party integration behavior under load, and those are often exactly where a DR plan's hidden assumptions live
Staging environments are always identical to production, so this is not actually a meaningful distinction
Production testing is required purely for compliance paperwork, not for finding real gaps
Staging tests are more expensive to run than production tests in every case
questions.explain: A DR test that passes cleanly in staging can still fail against real production traffic because staging often can't reproduce production's real data volume, cache state, or third-party behavior under load.

questions.q: In the canary-style failover test described in this lesson, what happens if error rate or latency exceeds normal bounds during the initial small-percentage traffic shift?
options: The test is paused for a week before any further action is taken
Nothing happens automatically; a human must manually notice and decide what to do
An automatic, pre-tested rollback reverts the traffic shift immediately, without waiting on a human to notice and react
Traffic is immediately ramped to one hundred percent regardless of the metrics
questions.explain: The rollback is automatic and pre-tested specifically so it can revert the traffic shift the moment metrics go out of bounds, without depending on a human noticing in time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat a scoped production DR test that fails as a valuable outcome rather than a problem to avoid?
options: A failed test surfaces a real gap — an expired credential, a missed dependency, a rollback that didn't revert cleanly — before an actual, unscoped disaster finds that same gap with no controlled way back
Failed tests are valuable only because they generate metrics for a dashboard, not because they reveal anything real
A failed test means the dependency graph was wrong and should be deleted
Failed tests are discouraged in this lesson in favor of only running tests that are known to pass
questions.explain: A scoped test that fails is doing exactly what it should: finding a real gap under controlled conditions, with a tested rollback available, instead of an uncontrolled real disaster finding that same gap later.
